# ELE680 — SAC width comparison: 2×256 vs 2×512 vs 2×1024 (HalfCheetah-v5)

*Generated by `analysis/plot_width_comparison.py`; every number below is computed from the tracked run files
(nothing is hard-coded). **Descriptive analysis of n = 3 independent training seeds per architecture; no claim of statistical
significance, superiority or inferiority is made.***

## 1. Experimental setup and scientific provenance

SAC (frozen algorithm and protocol) on HalfCheetah-v5, 1,000,000 environment steps, seeds 0/1/2, periodic evaluation every 25k steps
(5 deterministic episodes) plus one separate final evaluation (10 episodes). Only the hidden width of the two-hidden-layer MLPs
(actor, Q1, Q2) changes. Training was run on the UiS Gorina4 server.

| 2×256          |            256 |                217,870 |      1    | 1a9f240             | BASELINE_1M_seed0_20261009<br>BASELINE_1M_seed1_20261009<br>BASELINE_1M_seed2_20261009                                  |
| 2×512          |            512 |                828,942 |      3.8  | f25b3a0             | WIDTH_2x512_1M_seed0_20261010_134358<br>WIDTH_2x512_1M_seed1_20261011_004316<br>WIDTH_2x512_1M_seed2_20261011_143507    |
| 2×1024         |           1024 |              3,230,734 |     14.83 | e533a3c             | WIDTH_2x1024_1M_seed0_20261012_013236<br>WIDTH_2x1024_1M_seed1_20261012_101919<br>WIDTH_2x1024_1M_seed2_20261012_172628 |

**The three architectures were trained at three different Git commits** (`1a9f2405b5fdb9cffa379b72f569a0a3a01515e4`, `f25b3a0cb93da0a605b3dbac6254a866f83f664e`,
`e533a3c76ef069ffe37affc9a6a15ea2b1ae2e14`). The commits differ because the configurable-width code (`f25b3a0`) and then the 2×1024 configuration and
tests (`e533a3c`, which added only a config file and tests) were committed after the baseline. The default-width path is covered by
unit tests, but the earlier runs were not re-executed on the later commits. This is a documented confound, not an established equivalence.

## 2. Dataset validation (all nine runs passed)

Each run was checked, without repair or imputation, for: exactly one run directory; all six CSV/JSON files; HalfCheetah-v5; seed and
architecture (hidden width; the baseline omits `hidden_width`, read as the frozen default 256); exact scientific commit and clean tree;
parameter count; `completed` status at exactly 1,000,000 steps; `config.json` identical to the config in `metadata.json`; exactly 40 periodic
evaluations at 25k…1M (5 episodes) and one separate final evaluation at 1M (10 episodes); per-episode return arrays that reproduce the recorded
mean and population SD; metadata/CSV agreement for the final evaluation; exactly 994 training-metric rows at steps 6001, 7001, …, 999001 with finite diagnostics;
exactly 1,000 training episodes (1,000 steps each, steps 1000…1M, finite). Across all nine runs only `hidden_width`, `run_id` and `seed` differ in the configuration.
Final returns were also compared with the independent audit values in the unit tests (`RealSpecsAndNineRuns`).

Between-seed SD (sample, ddof=1) describes spread across training seeds; the within-run episode SD (population, ddof=0, across 10 evaluation episodes of a single trained policy,
52–176 across the nine runs) is a different quantity and is much smaller. Neither is a confidence interval.

Pairwise differences (unpaired; the same numeric seed in two architectures is **not** a matched sample):

| Comparison (wider − narrower)   |   Mean difference | Relative to narrower   |   Pooled SD |   Hedges' g |   Welch SE of diff. |   Exact permutation p |
|:--------------------------------|------------------:|:-----------------------|------------:|------------:|--------------------:|----------------------:|
| 2×512 - 2×256                   |            -260.9 | -2.19%                 |       489.9 |       -0.43 |               400   |                   0.6 |
| 2×1024 - 2×256                  |            -822.5 | -6.91%                 |      1181.1 |       -0.56 |               964.4 |                   0.4 |
| 2×1024 - 2×512                  |            -561.6 | -4.82%                 |      1178   |       -0.38 |               961.8 |                   0.6 |

- The mean final return is lower for each wider network (-260.9 for 2×512, -822.5 for 2×1024, relative to 2×256),
  but every difference is smaller than the between-seed SD of the 2×1024 group (1,595), and the seed ranges overlap
  (2×256: 11,336–12,250; 2×512: 11,216–12,167; 2×1024: 9,846–12,883).
- Exact permutation tests are exploratory. With 3 vs 3 seeds there are only 20 relabelings, the smallest attainable two-sided p is 0.10, and no pair can reach conventional
  significance whatever the data. A large p does **not** show equivalence either.
- The 2×1024 group is far more dispersed: coefficient of variation 0.144 vs 0.042 and 0.041.
- The periodic evaluation at 1M steps (5 episodes) uses the same deterministic episode seeds as the final evaluation and is not independent of it; the headline comparison uses the 10-episode final evaluation only.

## 5. Variability and stability diagnostics

### 5.1 Is the 2×1024 seed-2 advantage progressive or concentrated?

| Architecture   | SD 25k–250k (range)   | SD 275k–725k (range)   | SD 750k–1M (range)   |   SD at 1M |
|:---------------|:----------------------|:-----------------------|:---------------------|-----------:|
| 2×256          | 353 (661)             | 238 (464)              | 508 (961)            |        520 |
| 2×512          | 478 (931)             | 763 (1,440)            | 778 (1,536)          |        476 |
| 2×1024         | 1,285 (2,480)         | 1,498 (2,935)          | 1,560 (3,037)        |      1,596 |

(Entries: mean between-seed sample SD of the periodic mean return, and in brackets the mean max–min range across seeds, over the 10 / 19 / 11 evaluations of each phase.)

- In 2×1024, seed 2 has the highest 5-episode mean in 95% of the 40 evaluations and seed 0 the lowest in 97.5%.
  The max–min range across seeds is already 1,381 at 25k steps and 3,144, 1,098, 3,057 at 250k, 500k, 1M.
  The between-seed SD is high from the first phase onward (1,285 early, 1,560 late),
  versus 353 / 508 (2×256) and
  478 / 778 (2×512).
  So the observed separation is **not concentrated in late training**: the seed ordering is established within the first few hundred thousand steps and then largely persists. Whether this reflects the initial network/replay randomness of each seed cannot be told from three seeds.
- At 1M steps the final-evaluation gap between the highest and lowest 2×1024 seed is 3,037 return units, about 1.9 between-seed SDs of that group.

| Architecture   | Plateau: mean of 750k–1M evals   | Slope 500k–1M (return per 100k steps)   | SD of 750k–1M evals   | Max drawdown            | Evals after 500k with low-return outlier episode¹   |
|:---------------|:---------------------------------|:----------------------------------------|:----------------------|:------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| 2×256          | 11,726.2, 11,023.9, 11,929.7     | 345.0, 116.6, 299.7                     | 389.8, 260.2, 312.8   | 536.3, 714.3, 482.8     | 0, 0, 0                                             |
| 2×512          | 11,254.1, 12,043.0, 10,556.8     | 332.0, 191.9, 264.4                     | 422.5, 222.9, 889.2   | 475.7, 530.5, 2,377.9   | 0, 0, 2                                             |
| 2×1024         | 9,542.9, 10,378.4, 12,525.0      | 284.1, 250.0, 391.8                     | 267.1, 402.7, 311.6   | 818.6, 1,588.3, 2,389.4 | 0, 1, 1                                             |

¹ Low-return outlier episode: an evaluation episode whose return is below 0.5 × the median episode return of the same 5-episode evaluation. Descriptive heuristic only.

- Different 2×1024 seeds sit at different levels in the last 250k steps (plateau means above). The 500k–1M least-squares slopes are positive for all nine runs
  (smallest 117 per 100k steps), so none of the runs has clearly stopped improving; a "plateau" here is a level reached at 1M steps, not a demonstrated asymptote.
- Largest drawdown below the running best: 2×256 483–714, 2×512 476–2,378, 2×1024 819–2,389.
  The late within-run SD (750k–1M) of 2×1024 (267, 403, 312) is similar to 2×256, i.e. late-training noise of individual 2×1024 runs is not unusual;
  the group's large spread is between runs, not within a run's late curve.

### 5.2 Evaluation drops and optimisation diagnostics

A *drop* is a fall of more than 1,000 in mean periodic return versus the previous evaluation. For each drop, the maximum of the critic loss and critic gradient norm in the preceding 25,000 training steps is divided by that run's median.

| 2×1024         |      2 |              1 | 731001                             |            784.97 |                34.18 |                  17.58 |

| Architecture   | Median critic loss   | Median mean-abs Q   | Median critic grad norm   | Median α            |
|:---------------|:---------------------|:--------------------|:--------------------------|:--------------------|
| 2×256          | 44.0, 45.7, 40.1     | 712.0, 733.8, 733.0 | 1,581.0, 1,590.9, 1,657.1 | 0.280, 0.256, 0.265 |
| 2×512          | 22.7, 37.7, 32.2     | 726.6, 757.5, 680.9 | 1,249.6, 1,431.0, 1,074.1 | 0.215, 0.284, 0.247 |
| 2×1024         | 14.5, 19.8, 34.2     | 544.6, 584.7, 785.1 | 708.8, 839.9, 1,410.5     | 0.189, 0.278, 0.280 |

- Spike events (a contiguous run above 10× the centred 25-point rolling median) occur in all three architectures. The largest logged critic loss in the study is 784.97 (2×1024 seed 2); it is finite, belongs to a single
  logged value (17.6× its local median, spike event at step 731001), and the policy shows no matching evaluation drop around it
  (periodic means 12,013 at 725k and 12,020 at 750k). That is not evidence of divergence.
- 6 evaluation drops occur in total; 0 of them have a critic-loss spike event in the preceding window. The window ratios (table) are close to each run's typical value for most drops; 2 drop(s) (2×512 seed 2) have a critic-loss or gradient-norm window maximum more than twice the run's typical window. With at most 3 drops per run this is anecdotal: **the data do not establish a temporal link between evaluation drops and these diagnostics**, and any such link would be an association, not a demonstrated cause.
- Pooled over the nine runs (351 evaluation intervals), the Spearman rank correlation between the change in return and the critic-loss (critic-gradient-norm) window ratio is -0.33 (-0.37),
  but it falls to -0.06 (-0.02) when only intervals after 250k steps are used. The early negative value reflects training phase
  (returns rise fastest when losses are still small), not a mechanism. This analysis is **exploratory**: pooling runs and consecutive intervals ignores temporal dependence (the intervals are autocorrelated and their windows overlap), so the effective sample size is much smaller than 351, no p-value is reported, and the coefficients are descriptive only — a rank correlation would not be evidence of causation even if it were larger.
- Across architectures, median critic loss, critic gradient norm and mean |Q| are lower for 2×1024 than for 2×256 in this sample, and within 2×1024 the best-performing seed has the *largest* loss, |Q| and gradient norm.
  Q-value magnitude scales with return, so larger |Q| in the highest-return seed is expected and does not indicate instability.
- The entropy coefficient α is auto-tuned; its run medians (table) are similar for most runs, but 2×1024 seed 0 follows a visibly lower α trajectory for much of training and seed 1 ends higher than any other run (figure 05). Three seeds cannot show whether this relates to the seed-level return differences.

## 6. Compute and network scaling

| Architecture   |   Parameters |   × 2×256 | Runtime h (seeds 0, 1, 2)   |   Median runtime excl. flagged (h) | Final cumulative SPS   | Median interval SPS   |
|:---------------|-------------:|----------:|:----------------------------|-----------------------------------:|:-----------------------|:----------------------|
| 2×256          |      217,870 |      1    | 5.29, 5.08, 12.33           |                               5.19 | 52.5, 54.7, 22.5       | 51.4, 53.7, 22.5      |
| 2×512          |      828,942 |      3.8  | 5.05, 4.82, 5.04            |                               5.04 | 55.1, 57.6, 55.2       | 54.0, 56.8, 53.8      |
| 2×1024         |    3,230,734 |     14.83 | 5.26, 5.21, 5.18            |                               5.21 | 52.8, 53.4, 53.7       | 52.5, 52.0, 52.7      |

- Parameters grow 3.80× (2×512) and 14.83× (2×1024) relative to 2×256, whereas the median runtimes excluding the flagged run are 5.19, 5.04 and 5.21 h:
  runtime is nearly flat in width over this range on this hardware. This is an observation, not a controlled measurement.
- Runs flagged as more than 1.5× the median of all nine runtimes (5.18 h): `2×256 seed 2`. In `2×256 seed 2` the interval throughput falls from a median of 53.6 to 22.3 steps/s by step 81,001 and does not recover (figure 03): an abrupt, persistent change that is not a width effect (the other eight runs show no such change), but its cause was not recorded.
  The all-seed 2×256 runtime mean (7.57 h) is distorted by this run.
- Runtimes of 2×1024 (5.26, 5.21, 5.18 h) and 2×512 (5.05, 4.82, 5.04 h) differ by +5.0% in the means (every 2×1024 run is slower than every 2×512 run);
  this is consistent with a small width cost, but runs were executed at different times on a shared GPU server whose load was not recorded, so it cannot be attributed to width.
- Peak sampled GPU memory of 417 MiB per 2×1024 run was reported by the independent audit; the GPU-monitoring CSVs remain on Gorina4 and are **not** part of the tracked dataset, so this number is not verified here, it is a sampled value (not a hardware maximum), and no GPU-utilisation series is shown.
- Return versus parameters and versus runtime are shown in figure 08. Final return does not increase with parameter count in this sample, and with essentially constant runtime there is no meaningful "return per unit compute" trade-off to extract from three noisy runs.

## 7. Discussion and alternative explanations

**Observed:** the mean final return is 11,906 (2×256), 11,645 (2×512) and 11,084 (2×1024); the 2×1024 group has 3.2× and 3.3× the between-seed SD of 2×256 and 2×512; the best and worst 2×1024 seeds are 3,037 apart at 1M steps, an ordering that appears early and persists.

**Why the strong 2×1024 seed-2 result does not show that wider networks are better.** That run reached 12,883, the highest final return of all nine runs, yet the other two 2×1024 runs are the lowest and second-lowest of the nine (9,846, 10,522). One seed out of three is a sample of size one for the claim "this architecture can reach high return": it shows that high return is *attainable*, not that it is *typical*. It exceeds the best seed of the narrower networks (12,250) by 633.

**Why the lower 2×1024 mean does not show that wider networks are worse.** With a between-seed SD of 1,595 and n = 3, the standard error of the 2×1024 mean is about 921, comparable to the observed mean differences to the other architectures (823 and 562); the smallest attainable permutation p-value is 0.10; and
the two lowest 2×1024 seeds are still improving at 1M steps (positive late slopes), so the 1M-step comparison may favour architectures that learn faster.

**Alternative explanations (none tested here):**
1. Ordinary training-seed variability (initial weights, replay-buffer sampling, environment randomness) — the most economical explanation for a high-return outlier among three seeds.
2. Evaluation noise: the final evaluation uses only 10 deterministic episodes and the periodic ones only 5; within-run episode SDs are small relative to the between-seed spread, so evaluation noise alone is unlikely to explain the 2×1024 seed differences, but it adds to the visible dips of individual evaluations.
3. Optimisation effects of a fixed learning rate and target-update rate that were not retuned for width; larger networks often need different learning rates or initialisation scales. The 2×1024 critics and policies here use the same hyperparameters as 2×256.
4. Differences in the auto-tuned entropy coefficient (section 5.2) leading to different exploration regimes per seed.
5. Different Git commits per architecture and a shared, uncontrolled compute environment (runtime only; the learning dynamics are not expected to depend on server load).

## 8. Scientific limitations

- n = 3 training seeds per architecture; exact permutation tests cannot reach p < 0.10; standardised effect sizes from three seeds are very imprecise; bands in the figures are descriptive and not confidence intervals.
- One environment (HalfCheetah-v5), one hyperparameter setting, three widths with fixed depth 2, 1M steps (several runs still improving).
- Architectures were trained at different commits; baseline seed 2 had an unexplained runtime anomaly; shared-GPU load, peak GPU utilisation and other possible confounds of the server are not in the tracked data.
- The same numeric seed in different architectures is not a matched sample (no paired analysis was performed).
- The rank correlations between return changes and critic diagnostics pool nine runs and consecutive, temporally dependent intervals; they are exploratory, carry no inferential weight, and are confounded by training phase.
- Drop/spike/outlier criteria are descriptive heuristics with arbitrary thresholds (1,000 return, 10× rolling median, 0.5× evaluation median); they do not identify causes.
- Training diagnostics are logged every 1,000 steps and smoothed in figures; single-point spikes can be hidden by smoothing (figure 04 shows the raw values).

## 9. Conclusions (supported by the measured data)

1. All nine runs validate. In this experiment, increasing the hidden width from 256 to 512 to 1024 did **not** increase the mean final return (11,906 → 11,645 → 11,084) or the sample-efficiency proxy
   (9,912 → 9,560 → 8,925); the differences are within or near seed-to-seed variation and are not statistically testable with n = 3.
2. The 2×1024 group differs mainly in its **between-seed spread** (1,595 vs 497 and 482), which is visible from the earliest evaluations and persists; it is not a late-training effect.
3. No evidence was found that large critic losses (maximum 784.97) or evaluation drops reflect divergence or are demonstrably linked to each other; all logged diagnostics are finite and no run shows a persistent collapse of return.
4. Runtime was essentially independent of width over a 14.8× parameter range on this shared hardware (observational).
5. The data are compatible with the project hypothesis that naive width scaling does not guarantee improvement, but they cannot establish it, nor the opposite; more seeds, width-specific hyperparameter tuning and a common code revision are needed for firm conclusions.

## 10. Files and reproduction

Figures (PNG + PDF): `01_learning_curves_comparison`, `02_final_returns`, `03_throughput_and_runtime`, `04_critic_loss`, `05_entropy_alpha`,
`06_mean_abs_q_and_critic_grad_norm`, `07_return_difference_over_training`, `08_variability_and_scaling`.
Tables: `width_comparison_per_run.csv`, `width_comparison_checkpoints.csv`, `width_comparison_periodic_aggregate.csv`, `width_comparison_stats.json`.

Reproduce (repo root, local plotting environment; no training, no GPU):

```
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m unittest discover -s analysis/tests -v
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe .\analysis\plot_width_comparison.py
```

Text outputs and PNG files are regenerated byte-identically; PDF files embed no timestamp but may differ with matplotlib versions.
